en: The Manchus crossed Altay,
Drawing bows, making rain,
Firing shots, making hail.
Their men with iron-rope nets
Had encircled them,
Their men all armed with daggers.
Thrusting spears, Baltay striking,
I saw them grapple once.
The two champions went among them;
I saw them fight once!
Earth rained, dust blazed,
The Chinese surged in waves.
Many wrestlers entered the fray.
‘Precious Baltay has died,’
That is what I think now.
‘Once they cut those two down,
They will surge swiftly upon us,’ I thought.
I utterly despaired of life:
‘They will encircle us.’
See the ants, see the flood,
Attacking Kutubiy,
See the people who surrounded him!
‘They have destroyed them both together.
Kutubiy brought good fortune;
They have cut off his head,’ I thought,
And gave up hope for Kutubiy!”
Thus, about Akbaltay
And Kutu, the plight of those two,
He heard from wealthy Jakyp.
When he heard from wealthy Jakyp,
He roused himself like a lion,
Praying to his Allah:
“I will gird my waist firmly.
If these Kalmyks face me,
I will chase them as far as Beijing.
Smashing their stone-badged officials,
How can I fail to conquer them?
Shattering them to fragments,
How can I fail to bring
Havoc upon Beijing!
If we should happen to die,
If we should happen to leave this world,
Let me raise a mighty battle,
Destroying their strongest,
Let me avenge the blood of those two!
Living on without dying,
What inheritance would I attain?
Against the grim-faced Black Kalmyks,
Let me fight to the end!
Let me mount Toruchaar.
The Black Kalmyks who provoked us,
Let me drive them as far as Kakan!
The Chinese seem eager for it.
How can I fail to fight and shatter them?
This pig seems eager for it.
Let me break his eagerness!
The swarming infidels,
Let me sweep them as far as Kakan!
Like black spiders in Beijing,
These Chinese have multiplied, have they not?
The vast Kyrgyz, the numerous people,
From the beginning, raiding and overwhelming them—
These Chinese have grown accustomed to that.
Without dying or perishing, to this pig
How can I give my comrade?
Against the swarming Black Chinese,
Let me try making battle!
Your Kalmyks provoke your fury;
Let me drive them as far as Khangay.
If fighting is such a fine thing,
Let me try grappling with them!
I will bring abundant torment.
Akbaltay and Kutu,
If I myself reach them now,
I will free and rescue them!
The black-hearted Chinese,
If I do not drive them as far as Beijing,
Let me die rather than live!
Rather than walk about alive,
Let me sink away unborn!
Until the soft-stemmed stalks ripen,
Until the autumn gossamer flies,
Fighting hard for six months,
Thrusting spears and breaking their ranks,
Falling to a shot if my death comes,
I will gird my waist securely.
Let seven milek surge upon me;
I alone will attack the army!
While Manas is alive,
The Chinese cannot destroy and slaughter them.
These forty households of Kyrgyz,
The Chinese cannot destroy and take them.
They are no Chinese who can divide us;
I am no Manas who will let us be divided!
I will fight and wreak havoc.
Of the seething Manchus,
Not their horses—I, Manas,
Will raid and take their cattle!
I will see how they surge upon me.
Standing without fleeing, fighting,
I will die fighting here, at this very place!”
So saying, Khan Manas
Broke away from his caravan,
His blue-maned fierceness showing.
His companions were forty wrestlers.
Manas the leopard, favored by Kydyr,
Will bring great battle on the Chinese.
He had received letters from many places.
He is the leopard, he is the lion,
Called the Supremely Renowned,
A resourceful sultan, his name great—
No one like him arises among men,
Never shrinking back from a man,
Never turning back from death.
Born with fortune complete,
Born an exceptional blue-maned lion.
The Forty Chilten companions supported him.
That dear one visited by Kydyr,
No description could be made of him.
He grieved when ease was mentioned;
Know from this that he was a lion:
He rejoiced when death was mentioned.
Of that impulsive champion,
Who confounded the whole wide world,
Which deed shall we tell,
Of generous Manas the champion!
Of the skillful one among spearmen,
Which deed shall we tell,
Who confounded the whole wide world,
That mighty one created as a lion!
To his father, wealthy Jakyp,
Having heard of the hardship,
The immeasurable exhaustion:
“Alas, father, what are you saying!
If my death has come, I will die.
Against the Black Chinese ahead,
I will try grappling!
Without my dear life dying and vanishing,
Of my forty-household Kyrgyz people,
Letting their strongest be slaughtered,
Letting their weakest be taken as booty,
How can I withdraw alive!
I will thrust my spear and break their ranks.
For the people lying in humiliation,
If fate comes, I will fall to a shot!
While I still have life to spend,
Until I die and fade away,
Until my true death arrives,
Until my eyes close,
Of the overbearing Black Kalmyks,
How can I submit to their words?
The forty hearths in my charge,
Without fighting a battle of destruction,
How can I hand over as booty?
To their great lord, to their khan,
Swarming like ants,
To all the multitude of Chinese,
The forty Kyrgyz households, that small people,
How can I hand them over as booty?
Alas, father, what are you saying?
Who will listen to these words of yours!
When you were driven to Altay,
You seem to have made it your homeland.
The Black Kalmyks and Manchus
You seem to have made your people.
By remaining here in Altay,
What inheritance will we attain?
Rather than turn our necks in submission alive,
Of the Black Kalmyks and Manchus,
Rather than endure their oppression,
Let us die in slaughter!
The Kalmyks seem eager for it.
Let me enjoy the clash of battle!
If I have the strength, let me fight,
Let me throw myself back and wage war.
If Akbaltay has let himself be caught,
And especially if Kutubiy has died,
Let me bring a mighty slaughter.
If those two have been captured,
Fighting as far as Beijing,
Let me free and rescue them!
If the Black Manchus surge upon us,
Standing face to face,
Firing guns, drawing bows,
Facing them in a long battle,
Let me bring grievous suffering.
Against the Chinese who pour out fierce wrath,
Let me go and face them.
My adversary is Kakan-Chin;
How can I fail to fight!”
So saying, the leopard,
At whose sight attention was drawn,
Spoke many words to Jakyp:
“Alas, father, what are you saying?
You have no wisdom, no sound words;
You seem to have come to ruin.
Your honor has fled, your dignity gone;
You seem to have become worthless.
When the Chinese took the Kyrgyz,
Breaking and smashing your court,
When they took it as booty,
Destroying your girls and women,
When they brought devastation,
Then you grew afraid, wealthy Jakyp,
And seem to have become worthless.
Driven away from Ala-Too,
You moved away from Ala-Too.
Not remaining alive, Akbaltay,
You were extinguished that very moment!
I am pained by what you say.
Wealthy father, I have lost hope in you.
Does a warrior not die by the enemy?
Do those who remain not carry on living?
Against the infidels like black spiders,
Against the warrior at full strength,
I will charge and wage battle.
Without fleeing, fighting for six months,
My wretched people of forty households
I will free and rescue!
I will slaughter those who provoke us.
If mighty Allah supports me,
For the people who came wandering,
I will sacrifice myself utterly.
I will seize their finest men.
Fighting a splendid spear-duel on the plain,
I will devour their strongest.
Upon these Chinese eager for it,
To bring a costly slaughter,
The small, scattered, wandering people
To free and rescue,
Struck by a jezail shot,
To die if fate arrives,
Against the assembled Black Manchus
To keep waging war.
His eyes flashed like a hungry lion's.
Without looking up or down,
The hero Manas was bold.
Without sparing his life from death,
Without considering this way or that,
He was a wrestler, he was a lion,
Created in this world,
A hero born beyond others.
Hearing the word from Khan Jakyp,
That upon Akbaltay and Kutubiy
The Kalmyks over there had gathered,
Hearing that they had taken them,
Toruchaar beneath him,
He whipped from side to side,
Spurring this way and that.
Riding a horse no shot could reach,
Wearing a coat no spear could pierce,
If mighty Allah decreed,
To bring a fierce clash,
Without sparing his bare life,
Khan Baltay and Kutubiy
To free and rescue—
